newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 2.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Dec 2.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH -- CHIRAC AND KOHL RESTATE SINGLE CURRENCY SUPPORT

France and Germany have confirmed their commitment to a single currency by restating their support for a stable franc-mark exchange rate. This comes ahead of a meeting on Monday at which European finance ministers will discuss fines for countries whose economies diverge from the single currency conditions. French President Jacques Chirac and German Chancellor Helmut Kohl have spelt out their conviction for a steady relationship between the two key continental currencies.
-- WATER INDUSTRY SINKS DIFFERENCES

The Water Services Association, which represents nine of the 10 large water and sewerage companies, and the Water Companies Association, the body for the small water supply companies, are about to settle their differences and form a joint organisation. They are believed to have agreed to form a new joint association only on the understanding that the merger is not a takeover by the larger companies.
-- LADBROKE PLANS ONE BILLION STG WRITE-DOWN

Property and leisure group Ladbroke is planning to write down the share capital of one of its subsidiaries by more than one billion stg. British registered Ladbroke US Investments was until recently the holding company for the group's Hilton hotels division but the Registrar of Companies was last week given details of plans to reduce its share premium account from 1.15 billion stg to 115,000 stg.
THE TIMES
-- ABBEY LEADS WAY TO DEARER HOME LOANS

Britain's second largest housing finance lender, Abbey National, is to raise its variable mortgage rates by a quarter point as a response to the Budget. The next two weeks could see a similar move by the Halifax and other major lenders. Abbey claims that savers are the main target of rate changes. They will be offered increases averaging 0.11 per cent from January the first. The rate rises relate to the last quarter-point rise in bank base rates six weeks ago.
-- BUSINESS PLANS TO REINFORCE 'BETTER DEAL FOR WOMEN' DRIVE

Business leaders are set to reveal gains made by companies that have taken part in Prime Minister John Major's initiative to improve opportunities for women in management, thus proclaiming the success of efforts to break female employment barriers and urge more small companies to follow. Heads of major UK companies will claim that measures taken to realise greater equality at work have brought benefits to men as well as women through more reasonable working hours and flexible working arrangements.
-- LANG LIKELY TO REFER BASS DEAL

It is believed that the Office of Fair Trading has ruled against the planned purchase of Carlsberg-Tetley by Bass. The deal would have cost 205 million stg and would create Britain's biggest brewer with a market share of 40 per cent. The OFT has sent its advice to the President of the Board of Trade and has suggested the deal be referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission.
THE GUARDIAN
-- SECRET PROBE INTO BTR DEALS

The DTI is conducting an inquiry into trading in the shares of BTR, the industrial conglomerate run by Ian Strachan. Investigators believe a ring of a dozen City figures benefited from advance knowledge that BTR was poised to take over its partly-owned associate, BTR Nylex, in the summer of last year. The case also includes the investigation of offshore investment vehicles. BTR has declined to comment and the DTI refuses to discuss individual cases.
-- EMAP POISED TO END BOARD ROW BY AXING REBELS

The publishing and radio group, Emap, is to face calls to beef up its board with two new independent non-executive directors, at the group's general meeting. The board is expected to succeed in its attempt to remove the company's two dissident non-executives, Ken Simmonds and Joe Cooke. Emap will receive the backing of institutional shareholders. A number of institutions have called for the pair to be replaced by two non-executive directors, while Emap's chairman, Sir John Hoskyns, has been criticised for his handling of the affair.
-- IOD TAKES TOUGH STANCE AGAINST MONETARY UNION

The Institute of Directors has launched an attack on claims that Britain would benefit from signing up for European monetary union. IoD economic research executive Stephen Davies dismisses suggestions that British membership of the single currency would mean higher growth, cheaper borrowing and lower unemployment. The reason for the IoD's attack is a recent pamphlet from the European Movement UK which argued in favour of British participation in the single currency.
THE INDEPENDENT
-- MORGAN GRENFELL TO PAY OUT COMPENSATION EARLY

It is expected that Morgan Grenfell will pay compensation to investors in its three scandal-hit European funds in January, earlier than the Easter target date set by the investment regulator Imro. This will be a relief to 90,000 investors who have placed 1.4 billion stg in the funds before trading in them was suspended for three days in early September. Morgen Grenfell is presently in negotiations with Imro and the accountancy firm hired by the regulator, Arthur Anderson, to establish the basis of the compensation payments.
-- FIRMS REVEAL IGNORANCE OF DISABLED RIGHTS

Research by the Institute of Employment Studies shows that four out of 10 employers have never heard of the Disability Discrimination Act, which comes into effect today and could lead to litigation against companies. Charities representing the disabled believe businesses are letting themselves in for court action from prospective employees who have been rejected for jobs and current employees who believe they have suffered discrimination.
-- LLOYDS BIDDERS SET FOR FINAL FIGHT

Gehe, one of the bidders in the 650 million stg battle for Lloyds Chemists, is set to publish its offer document this week. This comes soon after the first indication from rival bidder UniChem of the level of interest its cash and shares offer has elicited from shareholders. Observers believe one or both of the bidders will be forced to raise their terms to clinch the bid and that Gehe will spin the bid timetable out as long as possible to put maximum pressure on UniChem.
